units.title: Batteries, Magnets and Motors
units.blurb: Make electricity from a lemon, turn it into magnetism, then motion, then back into electricity, the way Volta, Henry and Faraday did.

units.title: Messages, Light and Radio
units.blurb: Send a message down a wire, make a wire glow, and hear a radio with no battery at all.

units.title: The Printing Press
units.blurb: Set type, ink it and pull the press, and see why one machine changed how the world shared ideas.

topics.title: A Lemon Battery, Like Volta's Pile
topics.short: Two different metals in a sour juice make a small voltage; cells in series add their voltages.
topics.trouble: Builders use two pieces of the same metal, or let the zinc and copper touch inside the lemon, and get nothing.

topics.title: A Nail Electromagnet, Like Sturgeon's and Henry's
topics.short: Current in a coil makes a magnet; more turns and more current make it stronger, and an iron core multiplies it.
topics.trouble: Builders leave the enamel on magnet-wire ends, so no current flows, or hold the connection so long the wire gets hot.

topics.title: A Homopolar Motor, Faraday's 1821 Idea
topics.short: A current crossing a magnetic field feels a push, F = BIL; arranged right, the push keeps a wire spinning.
topics.trouble: Builders squeeze the wire tight against the battery so it can't turn, or use a magnet narrower than the battery.

topics.title: A Hand Generator, Faraday's 1831 Discovery
topics.short: A changing magnetic field through a coil makes a voltage; faster changes and more turns make more.
topics.trouble: Learners expect a magnet sitting still inside a coil to make current, or expect a few turns to light an LED.

topics.title: A Telegraph, Like Morse's
topics.short: A key closes a circuit; an electromagnet far away clicks; dots and dashes carry letters.
topics.trouble: Learners send letters with no gaps between them, so the receiver can't tell where one letter ends.

topics.title: A Glowing Filament, Edison's and Swan's Problem
topics.short: Current heats a thin filament until it glows; in air it burns away, so lamps need a vacuum or a gas without oxygen.
topics.trouble: Learners think the bulb's glass makes the light, or that a brighter filament in air would simply last longer.

topics.title: A Crystal Radio with No Battery
topics.short: A coil and capacitor pick one station; a diode turns its radio wave back into sound you can hear in a sensitive earphone.
topics.trouble: Builders use ordinary earbuds, which are far too hungry for current, or a short antenna indoors far from any AM station.

topics.title: A Printing Press, Gutenberg's Way
topics.short: Backward metal letters, set and justified, inked and pressed, print a page the right way round, hundreds of times a day.
topics.trouble: Learners set the letters forward, so the page prints backward, or forget that every line must be filled out exactly to lock up.
